On this page

Rheology ​

Rheology is the relation between the stress a material carries and the rate at which it deforms. In a mantle-convection model it enters through one field, the viscosity η, and that field decides more about the outcome than almost any other input. It sets whether the surface moves as plates, as a single stagnant lid or in episodic overturns, how thick and how cold the lithosphere becomes, and how fast the interior loses its heat. This page first explains the physics behind the viscosity laws, then how MILEVA evaluates them.

Physical background ​

Why solid rock flows ​

The mantle is solid. It transmits shear waves and, over seconds to years, it deforms elastically. Over millions of years it flows, because at temperatures above roughly half its melting temperature a crystalline rock deforms by thermally activated creep. Atoms diffuse through and around the grains, and lattice defects (dislocations) glide and climb through the crystals. Each of these processes produces a strain rate that grows with stress and very steeply with temperature (Karato 2008; Turcotte & Schubert 2014).

The time scale that separates the elastic from the viscous response is the Maxwell time, tM=η/G. With a viscosity of 1021 Pa s and a shear modulus of about 70 GPa, the upper-mantle value of the preliminary reference Earth model (Dziewonski & Anderson 1981), tM is about 450 years. Convection evolves over tens of millions of years, so the interior can be treated as a viscous fluid, and elasticity only matters in the cold lid (see Visco-elasto-plasticity).

A creeping rock is described by an effective viscosity, the ratio of the deviatoric stress to twice the strain rate,

τij=2ηε˙ij,η=τII2ε˙II,

where τII and ε˙II are the second invariants of the deviatoric stress and strain-rate tensors. For a Newtonian mechanism η does not depend on the stress; for a non-Newtonian one it does, and the "viscosity" is simply the value that reproduces the current stress at the current strain rate. With η=1021 Pa s and a strain rate of 10−15 s⁻¹ (a plate speed of 5 cm/yr sheared over 1000 km gives 1.6×10−15 s⁻¹) the stress is 2ηε˙II=2 MPa, the order of magnitude of convective stresses in the interior.

Creep viscosity from composite_rheology (yield branch switched off, default clamps) along the code's geotherm, an adiabat of 1600 K potential temperature below a 100 km conductive lid, at 10−15 s⁻¹. Left: the stress 2ηε˙II it implies. Right: the Maxwell time η/G with G=70 GPa. Even the cells held at the upper clamp of 1024 Pa s relax within about 450 kyr, far below the 10 to 100 Myr of convection. Script: docs/scripts/fig_rheology_sections.jl.

Deformation mechanisms ​

Laboratory experiments on olivine, the dominant upper-mantle mineral, identify several creep mechanisms (Karato & Wu 1993; Hirth & Kohlstedt 2003). They differ in how the strain rate depends on stress τ and grain size d:

mechanismstrain rate scales asviscositywhere it matters
diffusion creepτd−m, m≈2-3Newtonian, grain-size sensitivehot mantle, small grains, low stress
dislocation creepτn, n≈3-3.5strain-rate weakening, grain-size insensitivehigher stress, larger grains, upper mantle and lid base
grain-boundary slidingτnd−mboth stress and grain-size sensitiveintermediate conditions
Peierls (low-temperature) plasticityexponential in τvery strongly stress dependentcold lithosphere at high stress
frictional sliding and fracturestress set by pressure, not by rateperfectly plasticthe brittle upper lithosphere

All the thermally activated mechanisms share an Arrhenius dependence exp⁡[−(E+PV)/RT], with activation energy E and activation volume V. For dry olivine E is about 300 to 375 kJ/mol in diffusion creep and 530 to 540 kJ/mol in dislocation creep, with a stress exponent of 3.5 (Karato & Wu 1993; Hirth & Kohlstedt 2003); the values each preset carries are listed on the Flow laws page.

Mechanisms that operate side by side in the same grains act in parallel. Each accommodates part of the deformation at the same stress, so their strain rates add, and at a common stress their viscosities combine harmonically, 1/η=∑k1/ηk. The weakest mechanism carries most of the strain. Which one that is depends on stress, grain size and temperature, and a deformation-mechanism map is a plot of exactly this competition (Karato 2008). Karato & Wu (1993) concluded that the upper mantle lies close to the boundary between diffusion and dislocation creep, which is why a composite law that keeps both is the usual choice.

The default reference-viscosity creep laws of composite_rheology at 1600 K and 3 GPa, with the grain size entering diffusion creep (cfg.evolveGrainSize = true). Left: the viscosity of the parallel combination; the white line is where diffusion and dislocation creep are equally strong. Right: the fraction of the strain rate carried by diffusion creep, ηduct/ηdiff, at 10−15 s⁻¹. At 1600 K the two mechanisms share the deformation equally near 1 mm grains, and a hotter mantle moves the boundary to larger grains. Script: docs/scripts/fig_rheology_sections.jl.

Near the surface a different limit applies. Cold rock cannot creep fast enough, and it fails by fracture and frictional sliding instead, at a stress that rises with the confining pressure and hardly depends on the strain rate. Laboratory friction coefficients of 0.6 to 0.85 hold for most rock types (Byerlee 1978). The strength of the lithosphere at any depth is the smaller of the brittle and the ductile strength, the "strength envelope" reviewed by Kohlstedt, Evans & Mackwell (1995). Convection models need effective friction coefficients well below Byerlee's values to break the lid into plates (Moresi & Solomatov 1998; Tackley 2000), which is commonly attributed to pore-fluid pressure and to weak, pre-existing faults.

How strongly the viscosity varies ​

The Arrhenius factor makes temperature the dominant control. Differentiating it gives ∂ln⁡η/∂T=−E/(RT2), so the temperature change that alters η by a factor 10 is ln⁡10RT2/E. The numbers below are evaluated with MILEVA's default composite-path parameters (table further down), at the reference temperature of 1600 K unless stated:

changediffusion creep (E = 300 kJ/mol, V = 6 cm³/mol)dislocation creep (E = 540 kJ/mol, V = 14 cm³/mol, n = 3.5)
temperature change for a factor 10163 K318 K (the exponent is divided by n)
cooling from 1600 K to 1000 K, at P=0×7.5×105×1.1×103 at fixed strain rate
pressure from 0 to 5 GPa×9.5×4.5
strain rate ×10no change×0.19
grain size ×2 (m = 3)×8no change

A cold lid is therefore many orders of magnitude stiffer than the interior. A convenient measure of this sensitivity is the Frank-Kamenetskii parameter θ=EΔT/(RTi2), with ΔT the temperature drop across the layer and Ti the interior temperature; eθ approximates the viscosity contrast across the layer. As the contrast grows, convection passes from a small-contrast regime through a sluggish-lid regime to the stagnant-lid regime, in which the cold top boundary layer stops taking part in the flow and the interior convects beneath it; Solomatov (1995) places the stagnant-lid regime above a contrast of order 104. Whether a planet has a stagnant lid, plates or episodic overturns is then decided by the competition between this temperature-dependent stiffening and the yield stress of the lid (Moresi & Solomatov 1998). With power-law creep the temperature and pressure terms are divided by n at a fixed strain rate, as the right-hand column shows, so the same activation energy produces a smaller contrast; Christensen (1984) studied convection with this combined temperature, pressure and stress dependence.

The default diffusion and dislocation laws of composite_rheology, each alone and normalised to its value at the reference state, at a fixed strain rate of 10−15 s⁻¹. Left: temperature at zero pressure; the dotted lines mark the 163 K and 318 K of cooling that raise each viscosity tenfold. Right: pressure at 1600 K; at 5 GPa the factors are 9.5 and 4.5, as in the table. Script: docs/scripts/fig_rheology_sections.jl.

Typical values ​

quantityvaluesource
Earth, average upper-mantle viscosity1020 to 1021 Pa s, increasing substantially into the lower mantleMitrovica & Forte (2004)
Venus, interior viscosity inferred from stagnant-lid scaling1020 to 1021 Pa sSolomatov & Moresi (1996)
mantle strain ratesof order 10−15 s⁻¹estimate above
rock friction coefficient0.6 to 0.85Byerlee (1978)
olivine activation energy300 to 540 kJ/molKarato & Wu (1993); Hirth & Kohlstedt (2003)

Venus has no plate tectonics today, and its surface is dry. Mackwell, Zimmerman & Kohlstedt (1998) found dry diabase, a proxy for the Venus crust, to be much stronger than earlier wet-rock data suggested, which favours a strong lid; this is why the crustal presets of the Flow laws page include their law.

Creep viscosity of composite_rheology with default parameters (yield branch off) on the geotherm of the figures above, at three strain rates, against the 1020 to 1021 Pa s inferred for the Earth's upper mantle and the Venus interior. Without layered activation parameters the pressure term makes the viscosity grow with depth until it reaches the upper clamp below about 900 to 1300 km. The defaults are generic values, not a calibration to either planet, so a planetary run sets them against the inferred range. Script: docs/scripts/fig_rheology_sections.jl.

How MILEVA builds the viscosity ​

The viscosity η that enters the Stokes operator is built once per time step (and again inside the nonlinear iteration) in step (2) of the time loop in main_SphCon.jl. There are two paths, chosen by cfg.useCompositeRheology:

pathcfg.useCompositeRheologyentry pointdepends on
simplefalse (default)compute_viscosity (physics/compute_viscosity.jl), optionally overwritten by frank_kamenetskii_viscosity! (utils/fk_viscosity.jl)T, depth layer, composition multipliers
compositetruecomposite_rheology (physics/composite_rheology.jl)T, P, ε˙II, grain size, composition, accumulated strain

Both end with the clamp η∈[ηmin,ηmax] (cfg.eta_min = 1e18, cfg.eta_max = 1e24 Pa s by default). Optional modifiers (visco-elasto-plasticity, damage) are then applied on top, in that order.

The two paths that build the viscosity in step (2) of the time loop, with the default values each stage uses. Schematic; the numbers are the defaults of MaterialProperties and SimConfig. Script: docs/scripts/fig_rheology_sections.jl.

The strain-rate invariant used throughout is

ε˙II=12(ε˙rr2+ε˙θθ2+ε˙ϕϕ2)+ε˙rθ2

in 2-D (the ε˙ϕϕ=Vr/r term only in the spherical annulus) and the full six-component form in 3-D (compute_strain_rate, utils/compute_strain_rate.jl). The 2-D routine returns a raw and a spatially smoothed invariant; the rheology uses the smoothed one, the dissipation diagnostic the raw one. compute_strain_rate guards the square root with a floor of 10−30 s−1 and composite_rheology floors ε˙II at 10−20 s−1, both far below mantle strain rates.

Simple path: layered Arrhenius ​

compute_viscosity evaluates a pressure-scaled Arrhenius law on a six-layer prefactor table:

η(T,r)=η0(ℓ)exp⁡[(E∗+V∗P)(1T−1Tref)],P=ρ0g(Rout−r),

where E∗ = mat.E_act_scale and V∗ = mat.V_act_scale are in kelvin and kelvin per pascal (an activation energy and volume divided by the gas constant), Tref = mat.T_ref, and T is floored at 300 K. The layer ℓ comes from get_layer(mat, r) (config/MaterialProperties.jl):

layerradius rangeprefactor fielddefault (Pa s)
1, D″r≤ R_DprimeDprime_eta01022
2, lower mantle≤ R_lowerlower_eta03×1022
3, transition zone≤ R_transtrans_eta01022
4, upper mantle≤ R_upperupper_eta01021
5, asthenosphere≤ R_asthasth_eta01020
6, lithosphereabovelith_eta01023

The layer radii default to Earth values and must be set for another planet. Setting all six prefactors equal and E∗=0 gives an isoviscous mantle, which is how the Hernlund & Tackley benchmark driver configures its isoviscous cases.

The 3-D method of compute_viscosity uses the same table with the exponent E∗(1/T−1/Tref), without the mat.V_act_scale term.

This path is a prescribed, Newtonian viscosity. It depends on temperature and depth but not on stress, grain size or strain history, which makes it the natural choice for benchmarks and for isolating thermal effects. Because E∗ is an activation energy divided by the gas constant, a mantle-like 300 kJ/mol corresponds to E∗≈3.6×104 K. The default mat.E_act_scale = 200 K is far smaller and gives an almost depth-layered viscosity; between 1600 K and 1000 K it changes η by only a factor 1.08. A run that relies on temperature-dependent stiffening on this path must therefore set E∗ (or use the Frank-Kamenetskii form below) explicitly.

After compute_viscosity, the simple path applies, in order:

  1. Frank-Kamenetskii (cfg.useFrankKamenetskii), which overwrites η entirely with one of two forms selected by cfg.fkForm:
"linearized":η=ηrefexp⁡[E1+T/Tref−E2],"simple":η=ηrefexp⁡[−θFKT−TsurfTcmb−Tsurf],

with fk_eta_ref, fk_E, fk_T_ref and fk_theta. Both are approximations to the Arrhenius law that keep the viscosity contrast bounded and controllable. The simple form is the exponential approximation named after Frank-Kamenetskii, linear in T in the exponent. The linearized form has an exponent proportional to 1/(1+T/Tref), which resembles the Arrhenius 1/T but stays finite as T→0, so the viscosity contrast is at most eE/2 on either side of ηref. The simple form gives a viscosity contrast eθFK across the layer; the Hernlund & Tackley variable-viscosity cases use it with θFK=ln⁡106=13.8155.

  1. Depletion stiffening (cfg.useDepletionStiffening): η←η[1+(ξ−1)min(Cdep/Fmax,1)] with ξ = mat.harzburgite_eta_factor (default 3) and Fmax = cfg.fertileFraction (default 0.30), the same factor the composite path applies.

  2. Crust factor (2-D, cfg.crustViscosityFactor ≠1): η←η[1+(fc−1)Xcrust], with the crust fraction Xcrust defined in Buoyancy and composition.

  3. Yield cap (cfg.useSimpleYield, exercised in 2-D only): simple_yield! in physics/compute_viscosity.jl caps the stress at the Drucker-Prager yield stress of the composite path, τy=min(C+μP,τmax) with the same MaterialProperties fields, by η←min(η,τy/2ε˙II). Unlike the composite path it acts at every temperature (cfg.yieldMinT is not applied). The viscosity is then nonlinear, so the time loop iterates it with the solve (Nonlinear iteration); the stagnant-lid example uses it with a depth-independent τy. validate! refuses it together with useCompositeRheology or a radial viscosity file.

Each step re-clamps to [ηmin,ηmax].

Left: compute_viscosity on a 300-cell column of the default shell, on the geotherm used above. With the default E∗=200 K the six-layer prefactor table sets the profile; with E∗=3.6×104 K (300 kJ/mol) the cold lid reaches the upper clamp and the hot deep mantle approaches the lower one. Right: frank_kamenetskii_viscosity! between the default surface and core-mantle-boundary temperatures (300 and 4000 K) with the clamps lifted, for the default linearized form and the simple form at two values of θFK. Script: docs/scripts/fig_rheology_sections.jl.

arrhenius_viscosity! (utils/arrhenius_viscosity.jl, cfg.useArrhenius) and apply_660km_jump! (utils/viscosity_jumps.jl) are standalone utilities for drivers and tests; main_SphCon applies the Arrhenius law above, and cfg.use660kmJump acts on the composite path (below).

Composite path ​

composite_rheology evaluates, in this order (the file header documents the same sequence).

The computation for one cell, stage by stage, with the default material parameters. Right: the value each stage produces for a cold lithosphere cell (1000 K, 1 GPa, 10−14 s⁻¹), which yields, and a hot mantle cell (1600 K, 5 GPa, 10−15 s⁻¹), which creeps; the final values equal what composite_rheology returns for those cells. Script: docs/scripts/fig_rheology_pipeline.jl.

1. Ductile creep ​

With lithostatic pressure P from mantle_pressure (the reference state of the selected compressibility mode) and T floored at 300 K:

ηdiff=η0,diff(ddref)mexp⁡[EdiffR(1T−1Tref)+PVdiffRT],ηdisl=η0,disl(ε˙IIε˙ref)(1−n)/nexp⁡{1n[EdislR(1T−1Tref)+PVdislRT]},ηduct=(1ηdiff+1ηdisl+1ηGBS+1ηP)−1.

Here

symbolmeaningunit
Tabsolute temperature of the cell, floored at 300 KK
Plithostatic pressure at the cell's depth below mat.R_surfPa
Rgas constant, cfg.R_GAS = 8.314J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹
E, Vactivation energy and activation volume of the mechanismJ mol⁻¹, m³ mol⁻¹
η0reference viscosity of the mechanismPa s
Trefreference temperature at which η=η0 (with P=0)K
d, dref, mgrain size, reference grain size and grain-size exponentm, m, -
ε˙II, ε˙ref, nstrain-rate invariant, reference strain rate and stress exponents⁻¹, s⁻¹, -
ηGBS, ηPgrain-boundary-sliding and Peierls viscosities, infinite unless switched onPa s

Where the exponents come from. These are laboratory creep laws written in a reference-viscosity form. A power law ε˙=Aτnd−mexp⁡[−(E+PV)/RT] solved for the stress and divided by 2ε˙ gives

η=12A−1/nε˙(1−n)/ndm/nexp⁡[E+PVnRT],

so a stress exponent n turns into a strain-rate exponent (1−n)/n and divides the Arrhenius term by n. Diffusion creep is the case n=1, for which the viscosity is Newtonian and scales with dm. Instead of the prefactor A, MILEVA prescribes the viscosity η0 that each law has at Tref, P=0, dref and (for dislocation creep) ε˙ref, which is easier to choose and to compare between mechanisms. The temperature term (1/T−1/Tref) vanishes at Tref, while the pressure term PV/RT is not referenced, so η0 is a zero-pressure value. In the dislocation law the grain-size factor is absent because dislocation creep does not depend on grain size. The harmonic sum ηduct is the parallel combination described in Deformation mechanisms, in which whichever mechanism is weakest at the cell's conditions sets the viscosity.

parameterfielddefault
η0,diff, η0,dislmat.diff_eta0, mat.disl_eta01021 Pa s
Trefmat.T_ref1600 K
E, V diffusion, upper / lowerdiff_E_upper/lower, diff_V_upper/lower300 / 200 kJ mol−1, 6 / 3 cm3 mol−1
E, V dislocation, upper / lowerdisl_E_upper/lower, disl_V_upper/lower540 / 300 kJ mol−1, 14 / 3 cm3 mol−1
n, ε˙refmat.disl_n, mat.disl_eII_ref3.5, 10−15 s−1
m, drefmat.diff_m, mat.diff_d_ref3, 1 mm

The lower-mantle values of E and V are used only when cfg.useLayeredActivationEnergy = true; otherwise the upper values apply everywhere. The grain-size factor is 1 unless cfg.evolveGrainSize is on (Grain-size evolution).

Two optional mechanisms join the harmonic sum: grain-boundary sliding (cfg.useGBS, parameters cfg.gbs_A, gbs_n, gbs_m and mat.gbs_E_upper/lower) and Peierls low-temperature plasticity (cfg.usePeierlsCreep, active only where T<1100 K; the law is mat.flowlaw_peierls, Mei et al. 2010 by default). Both default off.

Published flow laws

Instead of the reference-viscosity laws above, the diffusion and dislocation creep of the mantle, a crustal law where there is basalt, and the Peierls law can be taken from published laboratory experiments (Hirth & Kohlstedt 2003, Karato & Wu 1993, Mackwell et al. 1998, Rybacki & Dresen 2000 and others), by name. See Flow laws.

Lower-mantle offset. With cfg.use660kmJump = true, every creep law below cfg.depth660km is multiplied by a prefactor (lower_mantle_creep_prefactors) that divides out the jump the E/V switch itself produces at the interface (evaluated at the horizontal-mean T and P of the two rows that straddle it, lower_mantle_interface_TP) and multiplies by cfg.eta660kmFactor. The viscosity ratio across the interface is then exactly eta660kmFactor at the interface conditions, and the E/V switch and the yield-parameter switch are moved to cfg.depth660km rather than mat.R_lower.

The ductile branch of composite_rheology with default parameters, yield off and clamps lifted. Left: diffusion creep is independent of the strain rate and dislocation creep falls with slope (1−n)/n=−0.71; the harmonic sum follows the weaker law. Middle: diffusion creep scales as d3 (with cfg.evolveGrainSize = true), and the sum saturates at the dislocation value for large grains. Right: the geotherm between 300 and 1200 km with cfg.use660kmJump and cfg.useLayeredActivationEnergy on; the viscosity rises by exactly eta660kmFactor = 30 across the interface (30.3 between the two rows that straddle it). Script: docs/scripts/fig_rheology_sections.jl.

2. Composition factors ​

Applied to ηduct only:

ηduct←ηduct[1+(ξ−1)min(Cdep/Fmax,1)][1+(b−1)Cbas][1+(p−1)Cpile],

with ξ = mat.harzburgite_eta_factor (3), b = mat.basalt_eta_factor (0.1) and p = mat.tcpile_eta_factor (1). Cdep, Cbas and Cpile are the marker fields projected to cells (the previous step's values; see Melting and crust production). With cfg.depletionStiffensYield = true the depletion factor also multiplies the yield viscosity.

The three factors stand for three materials whose creep strength differs from that of fertile peridotite. Melt extraction removes water and the most fusible components, and the dry, depleted residue (harzburgite) is expected to be stiffer (Hirth & Kohlstedt 1996); ξ is its viscosity ratio at full depletion, reached when Cdep equals the fusible fraction Fmax, so a partly depleted cell is stiffened in proportion to how far its melting has gone. Basalt and the thermochemical pile material enter in proportion to their fractions. Each factor is linear in its fraction and equals 1 for pure fertile mantle; this is a simple mixing rule, chosen for transparency, rather than a law derived for a two-phase aggregate. When a crustal flow law is selected (mat.flowlaw_crust_diffusion or mat.flowlaw_crust_dislocation), it replaces the basalt factor b, and the code then blends the mantle and crustal viscosities in log⁡η by the basalt fraction (see Flow laws).

Left: the factor composite_rheology applies to the ductile viscosity of a mantle cell (1600 K, 3 GPa, 10−15 s⁻¹) as each composition field goes from 0 to 1 with the others at zero. Depletion stiffens linearly in Cdep/Fmax and saturates at ξ=3 once Cdep reaches 0.30; basalt softens to b=0.1; the pile factor is 1 by default. Right: with published flow laws (Hirth & Kohlstedt 2003 dry olivine, Mackwell et al. 1998 Maryland diabase for the crust) the viscosity is blended in log⁡η, and depletion acts on the mantle fraction only. Script: docs/scripts/fig_rheology_sections.jl.

3. Drucker-Prager yield ​

τY=min[max(Ceff+μP, 0), τmax],ηY=τY2ε˙II,

with cohesion mat.cohesion_upper/lower (20 / 60 MPa), friction coefficient mat.friction_upper/lower (0.2 / 0.3) and cap mat.maxYieldStress (300 MPa). Where T< cfg.yieldMinT (default 0, i.e. nowhere) the yield branch is switched off (ηY=∞). Setting cohesion and cap to Inf removes yielding altogether.

Continent material can carry its own law: when mat.continent_cohesion or mat.continent_friction is set (both default to NaN, which keeps the layer's values), the cohesion and friction of a cell are mixed linearly in its continent fraction cc,

C0←(1−cc)C0+ccCc,μ←(1−cc)μ+ccμc,

so the yield stress is the volume-fraction average of the two, the same rule the continent viscosity factor follows.

The yield viscosity ηY is the viscosity at which a cell deforming at its current strain rate carries exactly the yield stress. Wherever ηY is the smaller branch, the stress in the cell is therefore held at τY and any further loading goes into faster deformation rather than higher stress, which is the viscous representation of a rock that has failed. The yield stress grows with pressure through the friction coefficient μ, like the frictional strength of Byerlee (1978), and the cap τmax limits it at depth, where ductile creep takes over in reality. The default friction coefficients (0.2 and 0.3) lie well below Byerlee's laboratory range, in line with the reduced values that convection models use to obtain a mobile lid (Moresi & Solomatov 1998). As an illustration, at 30 km depth with ρ=3300 kg/m³ and g=9.8 m/s² the pressure is about 1 GPa and the default upper-mantle law gives τY=20+0.2×970≈210 MPa.

With cfg.useFullPlasticity = true the cohesion weakens with the accumulated plastic strain εacc carried on markers:

Ceff=C0[1−W(1−1fsw)],W=clamp(εacc−ε1ε2−ε1,0,1),

with fsw = cfg.strainWeakeningFactor (default 1, no weakening) and ε1,2 = cfg.strainWeakeningE1/E2 (0.5, 1.5). The driver adds ε˙IIΔt to each marker's eps_acc every step when the flag is on (see Damage, softening and healing).

Left: the yield stress of composite_rheology's Drucker-Prager branch (2ηYε˙II with the creep laws switched off) against depth, with the default upper-mantle parameters and the lithostatic pressure of mantle_pressure. It grows by about 6.5 MPa per km, reaches 210 MPa at 30 km and the 300 MPa cap at 43 km; Byerlee's friction of 0.6 without cohesion is shown for comparison. Right: with cfg.useFullPlasticity = true the cohesion weakens between ε1=0.5 and ε2=1.5, for three values of cfg.strainWeakeningFactor; at 10 km only the 20 MPa cohesion is reduced, the pressure term is not. Script: docs/scripts/fig_rheology_sections.jl.

4. Combination, clamp and smoothing ​

cfg.viscosityCombination selects η=min(ηduct,ηY) ("min", default, the form of Tian et al. 2023 Eq. 6) or the harmonic mean 1/(1/ηduct+1/ηY) ("harmonic"). The result is clamped to [ηmin,ηmax] and then smoothed once in log10⁡η:

log⁡η~ij=(1−2wθ−2wr)log⁡ηij+wθ(log⁡ηi,j+1+log⁡ηi,j−1)+wr(log⁡ηi+1,j+log⁡ηi−1,j),

with wθ=0.08 (periodic) and wr=0.04 (one-sided at the walls) in 2-D, and a 14-12-14 stencil along θ only in 3-D (_smooth_viscosity). Being a convex combination in log space, it preserves the clamp bounds.

The "min" rule is the strength-envelope picture of Kohlstedt, Evans & Mackwell (1995). A cell deforms by whichever mode, creep or yielding, needs the lower stress at its strain rate, and the switch between the two is sharp. The harmonic mean treats the two branches as acting in parallel; it gives a smooth transition and, where the branches are equal, a viscosity half that of the "min" rule.

The bounds and the smoothing are numerical measures rather than physics. The clamp limits the viscosity contrast the Stokes solver has to handle; a cold lid in nature can be many more orders of magnitude stiffer than ηmax, so a run whose lid sits on the upper bound should be checked for sensitivity to it. The smoothing damps cell-to-cell jumps in log⁡η, such as those where the yield branch switches on in isolated cells.

The yield law is nonlinear

The yield viscosity ηY∝ε˙II−1, so the time loop iterates viscosity, solve and strain rate within the step on the composite path (see Nonlinear iteration). Keep cfg.picardMax at its automatic value or larger for any run with a finite yield stress. Inside the sweeps composite_rheology and the damage factor are reapplied; the visco-elasto-plastic reduction and the antisqueeze correction act on the first sweep.

cfg.useDruckerPrager and the dp_* fields belong to a separate helper, utils/drucker_prager.jl, used outside the time loop; validate!(cfg) refuses useDruckerPrager = true and points to the material fields above.

Viscosity along a geotherm (the code's adiabat at 1600 K potential temperature below a 100 km conductive lid), from composite_rheology with default parameters. Middle: each branch alone and the effective viscosity, the minimum of the branches inside the clamps; below about 700 km the default 300 MPa yield cap sets the value at this strain rate. Right: the effective viscosity at three strain rates, and the simple layered Arrhenius law of compute_viscosity on the same temperatures.

Assumptions and simplifications ​

The viscosity laws above rest on choices that are standard in mantle-convection modelling. They are listed here so that a result can be read with them in mind.

  • One isotropic viscosity per cell. Deforming olivine develops a crystal preferred orientation and an anisotropic viscosity (Karato 2008); MILEVA represents each cell by a single scalar η.

  • Viscous and plastic, not elastic, by default. Since the Maxwell time of the interior is centuries, elastic stresses are left out unless the visco-elasto-plastic modifier is on.

  • Lithostatic pressure. The creep and yield laws use the reference-state pressure of mantle_pressure at the cell's depth; the dynamic pressure from the Stokes solution is not added.

  • One strain rate for all mechanisms. The strain-rate-dependent laws are all evaluated at the cell's total ε˙II. For Newtonian laws this is exact. A stress-dependent mechanism that carries only part of the deformation would, in a combination at common stress, be evaluated at its own smaller strain rate and so be stiffer; the composite viscosity is therefore slightly lower than that of an exact common-stress combination where creep mechanisms share the deformation.

  • Lagged inputs. Composition fields and the strain rate come from the previous step or the previous nonlinear sweep; on the composite path the nonlinear iteration brings viscosity and strain rate into agreement within the step.

  • Fixed grain size and water content. The grain size is dref (or mat.flowlaw_grain_size, 1 mm, for the published flow laws) unless grain-size evolution is on, and the water measure of the published flow laws is one constant (mat.flowlaw_water), not a field.

  • No melt weakening. The viscosity does not depend on the local melt fraction.

  • Simple mixing of compositions. The composition factors are linear in the material fractions.

  • Numerical bounds and smoothing. ηmin, ηmax and the log-space smoothing are there for the solver, not for the physics.

Two of the simplifications measured on the code. Left: the ductile viscosity of composite_rheology (default laws, 1600 K, 3 GPa, 1 mm) divided by the viscosity of an exact parallel combination in which the two mechanisms share one stress and their strain rates add, solved here by bisection. The two agree where one law dominates and differ by up to a factor 0.70 where they share the strain equally. Right: one row at about 30 km depth of a 40 × 120 field in which a band of cells and one isolated cell deform at 3×10−13 s⁻¹ and yield, before and after _smooth_viscosity. The smoothing widens and rounds the weak zones without leaving the clamp bounds. Script: docs/scripts/fig_rheology_sections.jl.

Tests ​

  • tests/test_composite_rheology.jl: the composite law against the formulas it documents and the physics each creep mechanism must obey.

  • tests/test_rheology_switches.jl: the depletion factor ξ, the yield temperature gate, the min / harmonic combination, the lower-mantle offset (horizontally averaged ratio equal to eta660kmFactor to a tolerance of 0.05) and depletionStiffensYield, checked on composite_rheology(...; smooth = false).

  • tests/test_fk_viscosity.jl, tests/test_arrhenius_viscosity.jl: the helper laws.

  • tests/test_depletion_projection.jl: depletion reaches the viscosity and the buoyancy when melting is off.
